title: Je suis, tu es…
en: Subject pronouns & the verb être (to be)
intro: Your first grammar lesson: the little words for *I, you, he, she, we, they*, and **être** (to be), the most used verb in French. Every highlighted example can be pointed at or tapped.

cases.label: tu es — you are (informal)
cases.rule: **tu es**: one person you know well. For strangers or several people, use **vous êtes**.

cases.label: il / elle est — he / she is
cases.rule: **il est** for a man or a masculine thing, **elle est** for a woman or a feminine thing. The **t** of *est* is silent.

cases.label: on est — we are (everyday)
cases.rule: **on** uses the same verb form as **il**: *on est*. In conversation it means “we”.

cases.label: nous sommes — we are
cases.rule: **nous sommes**. A little more formal than *on est*.

cases.label: vous êtes — you are (polite / plural)
cases.rule: **vous êtes**: one person, politely, or several people. Liaison: /vu.zɛt/.

cases.label: ils / elles sont — they are
cases.rule: **elles sont** for women only. **ils sont** for men or any mixed group.

cases.label: être + job or nationality (no article)
cases.rule: No article: *Je suis professeur*, *Il est anglais*. A woman adds **-e**: *anglaise*.

cases.label: être + adjective (agreement)
cases.rule: The adjective matches the subject: **+e** for feminine, **+s** for plural: *contente, contents, contentes*.

cases.label: être + place
cases.rule: **à** + a city (*à Lyon*), **au** + a masculine place (*au café*), **ici / là** (here / there).

cases.label: c'est — this is / it's
cases.rule: **c'est** + a name, or + **un / une / le / la** + noun: *C'est Léa*, *C'est un ami*.

cases.label: ne … pas — saying no
cases.rule: **ne** before the verb, **pas** after it. **ne** becomes **n'** before a vowel: *il n'est pas*.

cases.label: yes/no question (voice goes up)
cases.rule: Same words as the statement. Raise your voice at the end, and write **?**.

sections.title: 1. Subject pronouns: who?
text: A **subject pronoun** stands for the person (or thing) doing the action. French has two words for “you” and two for “they”.

head: French
English
When to use it
rows: one person you know well: a friend, family, a child
a man, or a masculine thing
a woman, or a feminine thing
a little more formal or written “we”
one person, politely — or several people

sections.tip: **ils** wins as soon as there is one man in the group: ten women and one man = **ils**.

sections.title: 2. Être — to be
text: **Être** is irregular, so learn its six forms by heart. You will use it in almost every conversation.

head: Form
English
Sounds like
rows: il est · elle est · on est
he / she / it is · we are

sections.tip: **es** and **est** sound the same (/ɛ/); only the spelling changes: *tu es*, *il est*.

sections.title: 3. Who you are: nationality and job
text: After **être**, a nationality or a job takes **no article**: *Je suis étudiant* (not “je suis un étudiant”).
Nationalities start with a small letter: *français*, *anglaise*. A woman adds **-e**.

sections.title: 4. Describing: être + adjective
text: An adjective after **être** matches the subject: add **-e** for a woman, **-s** for several people, **-es** for several women.
sections.tip: Listen: in *contente* you hear the **t** (/kɔ̃.tɑ̃t/), in *content* you don't. But *fatigué* and *fatiguée* sound the same.

sections.title: 5. Saying where you are
text: **à** + a city: *Je suis à Paris*. **au** (= à + le) + a masculine place: *Il est au café*. **ici** = here, **là** = here / there.

sections.title: 6. C'est… — pointing to someone or something
text: **C'est** (ce + est) means “this is”, “it's”, “he's” or “she's”. Use it before a name, or before **un / une / le / la** + a noun.
sections.tip: With an article, use **c'est**: *C'est un professeur*. Without one, use **il / elle est**: *Il est professeur*.

sections.title: 7. Saying no: ne … pas
text: Put **ne** before the verb and **pas** after it. Before a vowel, **ne** becomes **n'**.
sections.tip: In casual speech people often drop **ne**: *Je suis pas fatigué*. Understand it, but write **ne … pas**.

sections.title: 8. Asking yes/no questions
text: The easiest way: say the sentence with your voice going **up** at the end. In writing, just add **?**.
sections.tip: Statement ↘ *Tu es français.* — Question ↗ *Tu es français ?*

mistakes.why: Age uses **avoir** (to have), not être. You'll learn avoir in Unit 3.
No article for a job after **je suis / il est**.
Same sound, different spelling: **tu es**, **il est**.
In writing you need both **ne** and **pas**.

mistakes.wrong: Léa et Tom ? Elles sont là.
mistakes.right: Léa et Tom ? Ils sont là.

story.title: Le premier jour
story.en: The first day — Léa's first French class in Lyon.

lines.fr: {On est|etre-on} lundi matin. {Léa est à Lyon|etre-place}, dans une école de français.
lines.en: It's Monday morning. Léa is in Lyon, at a French school.

lines.fr: {C'est|etre-cest} le premier jour. {Elle est|etre-il-elle} un peu {fatiguée|etre-adj}, mais {contente|etre-adj}.
lines.en: It's the first day. She's a little tired, but happy.

lines.fr: Bonjour à tous ! Je m'appelle Marc. {Je suis professeur|etre-who}. {Vous êtes|etre-vous} tous là ?
lines.en: Hello, everyone! My name is Marc. I'm a teacher. Are you all here?

lines.fr: Bonjour, monsieur ! Je m'appelle Léa. {Je suis|etre-je} de Paris.
lines.en: Hello, sir! My name is Léa. I'm from Paris.

lines.fr: Bienvenue, Léa ! Et toi, {tu es|etre-tu} Hugo ?
lines.en: Welcome, Léa! And you — are you Hugo?

lines.fr: Non, {je ne suis pas|etre-neg} Hugo ! Je m'appelle Tom. {Je suis anglais|etre-who}.
lines.en: No, I'm not Hugo! My name is Tom. I'm English.

lines.fr: Pardon, Tom ! Et Hugo ? {Il n'est pas|etre-neg} là ?
lines.en: Sorry, Tom! And Hugo? He isn't here?

lines.fr: Non, {il est au café|etre-place}, avec Inès et Carla.
lines.en: No, he's at the café, with Inès and Carla.

lines.fr: Pas de problème. Inès et Carla, {vous êtes espagnoles|etre-question} ?
lines.en: No problem. Inès and Carla, are you Spanish?
And you, Hugo? Are you French?

lines.fr: Non, {je ne suis pas|etre-neg} français. {Je suis canadien|etre-who}, de Montréal !
lines.en: No, I'm not French. I'm Canadian, from Montreal!

lines.fr: Inès et Carla ? {Elles sont|etre-ils-elles} de Madrid. Léa et Tom ? {Ils sont|etre-ils-elles} de Paris et de Londres.
lines.en: Inès and Carla? They're from Madrid. Léa and Tom? They're from Paris and London.

lines.fr: {C'est une bonne classe|etre-cest}. {Les étudiants sont contents|etre-adj}, et {Marc est très content|etre-adj} aussi.
lines.en: It's a good class. The students are happy, and Marc is very happy too.
Right! Are we ready? Let's begin!

quiz.why: **on** takes the same form as **il**: *on est*.

quiz.q: Inès et moi, nous ___ de Madrid.
quiz.en: Inès and I are from Madrid.
Tom and Hugo, are you here?

quiz.q: You're speaking to your teacher, Mr. Martin. Which question is polite?
quiz.why: Use **vous** with people you don't know well, or to be polite.

quiz.q: Léa et Tom ? ___ sont de Paris.
quiz.en: Léa and Tom? They're from Paris.
quiz.why: A mixed group — even one man — is **ils**.
After **il est**, a job has no article.
No article, and **-ne** is added for a woman: *canadien → canadienne*.
**là** (with the accent) means here / there; **la** means “the”.

options: Nous ne sommes pas de Paris.
Nous sommes ne pas de Paris.
Nous ne sommes de Paris pas.
quiz.answer: Nous ne sommes pas de Paris.

quiz.q: How do you ask a friend “Are you French?”
quiz.why: Same words as the statement — raise your voice and write **?**.
